name: Enhanced rock weathering and ocean alkalinity enhancement
principle: Crushed silicate rock (basalt, olivine) is spread on land or added to seawater so it weathers faster and converts CO2 to bicarbonate. Strefler and colleagues estimated potentials of up to 95 Gt CO2/yr for dunite and 4.9 Gt for basalt on cropland and costs of about USD 60 per tonne CO2 for dunite and USD 200 for basalt. UNDO and Planetary are listed as developers.

process_steps.name: Spread on cropland or add to seawater

source.note: Strefler et al., Potential and costs of carbon dioxide removal by enhanced weathering of rocks, Environmental Research Letters 2018

costs.basis: dunite about 60, basalt about 200; paper published 2018, dollar year not stated

source.note: Strefler et al., Potential and costs of carbon dioxide removal by enhanced weathering of rocks, Environmental Research Letters 2018

advantages: India, Brazil, South-East Asia and China hold almost 75% of the potential (paper)
limitations: Measurement of real CO2 removal is hard (not quantified in source read)

sources.note: Strefler et al., Potential and costs of carbon dioxide removal by enhanced weathering of rocks, Environmental Research Letters 2018

reference_plants.name: UNDO enhanced rock weathering programme, UK farms (Scotland and northern England)
reference_plants.capacity: more than 141,000 t of crushed basalt spread on UK farms in 2023, expected over time to draw down about 37,000 t CO2 (projected, not yet measured); Microsoft-funded 25,000 t pilot (2023)

source.note: The Times, 13 Apr 2023 (Microsoft-funded 25,000 t pilot); trade reporting 29 Oct 2024 (141,000 t spread, ~37,000 t CO2 expected drawdown); read 2026-10-28

IEA ETP Clean Energy Technology Guide public dataset, row 'CO2 sequestration in inert carbonate materials (mineralisation)' TRL 2025 - mineralisation is the same carbonation chemistry; read 2026-11-16

notes: Process provenance: Documents the ERW chain and its quantification - sourcing and crushing silicate rock to raise reactive surface area, spreading on soils, and third-party monitoring, sampling and quantification of CO2 removed and stored as bicarbonate/carbonate.
